routes.description: Build a cumulative historical inference from reported appearances, their embodied interpretation, the empty tomb, apostolic sincerity, and comparisons with rival miracle claims.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these strands are historically credible and bodily resurrection explains their conjunction with fewer difficulties than the proposed alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The motion is supported if bodily resurrection is the best explanation of the cumulative historical evidence.

centralBridges.description: Individual and group appearance reports must provide credible evidence that Jesus was alive after his death.
The reported resurrection must concern the same embodied person who was crucified rather than disembodied survival or an ordinary vision.
The missing body, conversions, and costly proclamation must be jointly explicable within the resurrection account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The relevant sources and apostolic conduct must adequately support the sincerity and historical grounding of the testimony.
Material differences must prevent rival miracle testimony from neutralizing the resurrection evidence.

routes.description: Challenge whether the sources establish bodily appearances, a secure empty tomb, distinctive martyrdom evidence, or an inference standard consistently applied to rival miracle claims.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if central facts remain insecure, visionary or natural alternatives remain viable, or comparable testimony shows that the inference does not warrant bodily resurrection.

motionBridge.description: The motion is not established if the surviving evidence underdetermines bodily resurrection and remains compatible with materially plausible alternatives.

centralBridges.description: The surviving record must be tested for firsthand access, independence, chronology, and later narrative elaboration.
Sincere or even veridical visionary experiences must be distinguished from encounters with a physically resurrected body.
Temporary burial, relocation, theft, or uncertainty about the tomb must remain available where the evidence permits them.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Persecution must be tied specifically to informed bodily-resurrection testimony before it can support that conclusion.
Comparable religious testimony must be treated by a consistent evidential standard.

sections.title: Appearance Testimony
sections.rationale: The initial historical inference depends on whether reported individual and group encounters provide adequate grounds for concluding that Jesus lived after his death.

sections.title: Bodily or Visionary Resurrection
sections.rationale: The motion specifically requires physical resurrection, making the interpretation of Pauline language and developing appearance narratives indispensable.

sections.title: Rival Miracle Comparisons
sections.rationale: Comparisons with Mormon and other religious testimony test whether the evidential standard applied to resurrection reports is discriminating and consistent.

sections.title: Martyrdom and Witness Sincerity
sections.rationale: Costly commitment can bear on sincerity, but its relevance depends on what witnesses knew, proclaimed, and were specifically endangered for affirming.

sections.title: Empty Tomb and Competing Explanations
sections.rationale: A genuinely missing body supports the bodily inference only if the tomb tradition is credible and relocation or theft does not adequately explain it.

sections.title: Cumulative Historical Warrant
sections.rationale: The final burden concerns whether the selected evidence jointly makes bodily resurrection historically reasonable despite limitations in firsthand testimony.
